name: Vantablack Ops Liaison Jacket
description:
Vantablack doesn't issue tactical uniforms in the traditional sense. The Ops Liaison Jacket is designed to look like civilian outerwear — a trim, mid-length coat in flat matte black that reads as expensive street fashion until it doesn't. The exterior fabric is woven with Vantablack's signature light-absorption compound, not to the extreme of true VantaMat applications, but enough to make the wearer visually recede in low-light environments, reducing silhouette definition and making optical tracking systems struggle for clean acquisition. The jacket carries no visible corporate branding; the only identifying marker is a microscopic spectral tag in the left cuff, readable only by Vantablack-issued scanners.

Internally, the jacket is a different garment entirely. A network of sensor-filament threads maps the wearer's immediate environment and feeds data through a BCI port concealed within the collar seam. Pockets are shielded against RF scanning, and the lining includes a signal-dampening mesh that limits the wearer's electronic signature in monitored spaces. The jacket is cut to read as civilian across Tier 3 through 5 environments — it is not designed for the Shelf, where anyone wearing something that expensive without obvious corp affiliation becomes a target. Vantablack personnel who operate in lower tiers are typically issued cover garments to wear over the jacket. Possession without authorization is deeply inadvisable.
cultural_context: Vantablack has a reputation for existing in spaces it officially doesn't occupy. The Ops Liaison Jacket is part of that reputation — a garment that signals intelligence presence without confirming it. In M88's corporate circles, being approached by someone in a coat that eats light is understood as a meeting you don't discuss afterward.
story_hooks: A counterfeit version of the Ops Liaison Jacket is circulating in Tier 3 markets — it has the visual profile but none of the electronics, and someone wearing one is about to walk into a situation where Vantablack will assume they're an operative.
The spectral tag in a recovered jacket's cuff doesn't match any active Vantablack operative ID — it belongs to someone who was officially declared dead two years ago.

A journalist investigating corporate surveillance purchases what they believe is a replica jacket for a story on Vantablack's visual-stealth tech, and discovers the 'replica' is feeding data to an unknown receiver.
